Q: How does clustering differ from classification and semantic search?
explain: Classification predicts known labels using a defined target contract. Clustering discovers groups according to a representation and objective without supplying those class labels to the fit step. Search returns candidates relative to a query. An embedding can support any of these tasks, but it does not make them equivalent. A cluster identifier is arbitrary and can change after a refit; cluster 2 is not inherently the delivery category. Inspect source examples and evaluate whether the discovered grouping serves a real purpose before attaching a business name or workflow action.
example: Three message groups emerge without category labels. An analyst later finds that one reflects polite writing style rather than a support issue. A neat partition can be mathematically coherent and still unsuitable for routing.
takeaway: A discovered group is a hypothesis about structure, not a ground-truth class.

Q: Why must clustering begin with a representation, a distance and a usefulness question?
explain: Most clustering methods operate on geometry rather than understanding the product goal. Units, feature scaling, tokenization, embedding training and distance choice determine which items become neighbors. Euclidean distance on standardized numeric measurements answers a different question from cosine distance on normalized sentence embeddings. Normalize only when the chosen geometry calls for it, and handle zero vectors explicitly. Decide whether you want compact groups, density-connected shapes, a hierarchy or soft memberships before fitting. A two-dimensional plot is a diagnostic view, not the definition or proof of the grouping.
example: Messages share nearly all vocabulary but one includes a negation. A broad sentence encoder can place them nearby, while the desired grouping may depend on that decisive difference. Inspect representative and boundary examples instead of trusting vector proximity alone.
takeaway: The representation and objective jointly define what similar means.
